full_text: Kamran Razmovar presents another argument, claiming that the Bible doesn’t mention Armenians at all, which means ancient Armenia is a fabrication. But that’s not how the existence of countries and peoples is established. Now, let’s dispel this myth of Great Armenia, which supposedly included Jerusalem. According to Wikipedia, Great Armenia existed in the fourth century, while our records date back to about the fifth century. And somewhere in the middle of those 80 years, Jesus Christ was born in Bethlehem, by the way, close to Jerusalem. Strangely enough, not a single Armenian encountered Jesus. The Bible doesn’t mention anything about Armenians. There’s no mention of a Great Armenia; there are dozens of nationalities and ethnicities, but no Armenians or Armenias. We shouldn’t force that in; it says “the mountains of Ararat.” That’s a geographical term. The Gospel is not a list of all the peoples of the Near East. The absence of a people in the story of Christ’s life doesn’t mean they were absent from history. Moreover, the name Armenia is recorded about five centuries before Jesus was born. Around 520 BC, Darius I left the Behistun inscription. In the Old Persian text, the country is referred to as “Armina,” south of Armenia. The Encyclopaedia Iranica translates this as Armenia. Now, regarding Kamran’s claim that the Bible mentions Armenia but not Armenians—this is also incorrect when discussing biblical translations in general. In the King James Version of the Bible, in 2 Kings 19:37 and in the book of Isaiah 37:38, the phrase “land of Armenia” is used directly. In modern translations, “land of Ararat” is often used in these same places. This highlights the main problem with Kamran’s argument. Different linguistic and translation traditions can convey ancient geographical names differently. This is evident even in the Behistun inscription. Ancient Persian versions use the name Armina for the Babylonian region, which is an older Mesopotamian name “Urartu” that existed earlier in the same area. There are independent Greek testimonies as well. Herodotus in the fifth century BC mentions Armenians. Xenophon in the early fourth century BC repeatedly writes about Armenia and Armenians. Therefore, Kamran’s question of why Jesus didn’t meet Armenians historically proves nothing. Persian and Greek sources record Armenia and Armenians for centuries before Christ’s birth. And the attempt to prove the absence of Armenia by using the word “Ararat” collapses on the sources themselves. Kamran simply mixes different linguistic traditions and interprets the variation in names as the absence of a country.
